# gitwig_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/gitwig-core/2.3.14/gitwig_core/

## Expand description

Filesystem + git repository inspection.

This module owns both the “is this a git repo?” classification used by
the per-card indicator AND the richer detail collection used by the
Detail view. They share a single `collect_summary` helper so the same
libgit2 work doesn’t run twice.

The cheap `is_dir()` + `.git`-existence check still gates everything —
we only spin up libgit2 when both checks pass.

# turnkey_enclave_encrypt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/turnkey_enclave_encrypt/0.9.0/turnkey_enclave_encrypt/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#turnkey_enclave_encrypt)`turnkey_enclave_encrypt`

This crate contains primitives to encrypt and decrypt data, sent to and from Turnkey secure enclaves (see Enclave to [end-user secure channels](https://docs.turnkey.com/security/enclave-secure-channels)).

Encryption and decryption are “one-shot” using the HPKE standard ([RFC 9180](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9180/)).  Neither the client or the server should ever be reused to send/receive more than one message. We want to avoid the recipient target key being used more then once in order to improve forward secrecy; see [security profile](https://docs.rs#security-profile) section for important details and caveats.

The flows where encryption and decryption are relevant are:

- Authentication: [Email](https://docs.turnkey.com/authentication/email),[SMS](https://docs.turnkey.com/authentication/sms), or[Social](https://docs.turnkey.com/authentication/social-logins)logins return encrypted authentication bundles produced by Turnkey secure enclaves
- Key or Wallet export: key material (private key or wallet mnemonic phase) are encrypted by Turnkey enclaves to end-user public keys. See [Export Wallets and Keys](https://docs.turnkey.com/wallets/export-wallets#export-wallets-and-keys).
- Key or Wallet import: Turnkey enclaves send a bundle containing a signed public key, to which end-users encrypt their key material (private key or wallet mnemonic phrase). See [Import Wallets and Keys](https://docs.turnkey.com/wallets/import-wallets).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#authentication-bundles)Authentication bundles

```
use turnkey_enclave_encrypt::{AuthenticationClient, QuorumPublicKey};
let mut client = AuthenticationClient::new();
let target_public_key = client.target_public_key(); // can be used in auth activity params
let bundle = "<auth bundle>";
let decrypted = client.decrypt(bundle).expect("decryption should succeed");
```
If you persist client key material between initiation and decryption you may use `dangerous_from_bytes` to create an `AuthenticationClient`. Keep in mind the one-shot encryption semantics, you may not use the same client IKM to decrypt many different bundles.

```
use turnkey_enclave_encrypt::{AuthenticationClient, QuorumPublicKey};
let client_ikm = hex::decode("...private bytes from client...").expect("cannot decode client secret bytes");
let bundle = "<auth bundle goes here, it's a base58-encoded string>";
let decrypted = AuthenticationClient::dangerous_from_bytes(client_ikm)
    .decrypt(bundle)
    .expect("decryption should succeed");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#export-bundles)Export bundles

To decrypt an exported private key or wallet, use `decrypt_private_key` or `decrypt_wallet`:

```
use turnkey_enclave_encrypt::{ExportClient, QuorumPublicKey};
let mut client = ExportClient::new(&QuorumPublicKey::production_signer());
// Decrypt a wallet (result: string)
let wallet_mnemonic_phrase = client.decrypt_wallet_mnemonic_phrase("<bundle>", "<organization id>");
// Decrypt a private key (result: bytes)
let private_key = client.decrypt_private_key("<bundle>", "<organization id>");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#import-bundles)Import bundles

To encrypt private keys or wallets, use `encrypt_private_key_with_bundle` or `encrypt_wallet_with_bundle`. The resulting value is a string, ready to use as an activity param. The organization and user IDs need to match the organization and user who initiated import.

```
use turnkey_enclave_encrypt::{ImportClient, QuorumPublicKey};
let mut client = ImportClient::new(&QuorumPublicKey::production_signer());
// Encrypt private keys
let encrypted_key = client.encrypt_private_key_with_bundle(
    "<bytes to encrypt>",
    "<bundle>",
    "<organization id>",
    "<user id>",
).expect("encryption should succeed");
// Encrypt wallet seed phrase
let encrypted_wallet = client.encrypt_wallet_with_bundle(
    "<mnemonic phrase>",
    "<bundle>",
    "<organization id>",
    "<user id>",
).expect("encryption should succeed");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#running-test)Running test

`cargo test`[§](https://docs.rs#hpke-protocol-details)HPKE Protocol Details

[§](https://docs.rs#terms)Terms

- Encapsulated (“Encapped”) Key - the public key of the sender used for ECDH.
- Target Key Pair - the key pair of the receiver that the sender encrypts to the public key of. Only one message should ever be encrypted to the public key.
- Server - a server inside of the enclave; normally an enclave application.
- Client - a client outside of the enclave; normally a turnkey end user.
- Enclave Auth Key Pair - a key pair derived from the quorum master seed specifically for the purpose of authentication with clients.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This protocol builds on top of the HPKE standard ([RFC 9180](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9180)) by adding recipient pre-flight authentication so the client can verify it is sending ciphertext to a turnkey controlled enclave and the enclave can verify its sending ciphertext to the correct client. See the [security profile](https://docs.rs#security-profile) section more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#hpke-configuration)HPKE Configuration

- KEM: `KEM_P256_HKDF_SHA256`
- KDF: `KDF_HKDF_SHA256`
- AEAD: `AEAD_AES256GCM`
- INFO: `b"turnkey_hpke"`
- ADDITIONAL ASSOCIATED DATA: `EncappedPublicKey||ReceiverPublicKey`

[§](https://docs.rs#protocol-flow)Protocol Flow

[§](https://docs.rs#server-to-client)Server to Client

- Client generates target pair and sends clientTargetPub key to server. The authenticity of the clientTargetPub is assumed to have been verified by the Ump policy engine.
- Server computes ciphertext, `serverEncappedPub`=`ENCRYPT(plaintext, clientTargetPub)`and clears`clientTargetPub`from memory.
- Server computes `serverEncappedPub_sig_enclaveAuthPriv`=`SIGN(serverEncappedPub, enclaveAuthPriv)`.
- Server sends `(ciphertext, serverEncappedPub, serverEncappedPub_sig_enclaveAuthPriv)`to client.
- Client runs `VERIFY(serverEncappedPub, serverEncappedPub_sig_enclaveAuthPriv)`.
- Client recovers plaintext by computing `DECRYPT(ciphertext, serverEncappedPub, clientTargetPriv)`and the client target pair is cleared from memory. If the target pair is used multiple times we increase the count of messages that an attacker with the compromised target private key can decrypt.

Note there is no mechanism to prevent a faulty client from resubmitting the same target public key.

[§](https://docs.rs#client-to-server)Client to Server

- Client sends request to server for target key.
- Server generates server target pair and computes `serverTargetPub_sig_enclaveAuthPriv`=`SIGN(serverTargetPub, enclaveAuthPriv)`.
- Server sends `(serverTargetPub, serverTargetPub_sig_enclaveAuthPriv)`to client.
- Client runs `VERIFY(serverTargetPub, serverTargetPub_sig_enclaveAuthPriv)`.
- Client computes ciphertext, `clientEncappedPub`=`ENCRYPT(plaintext, serverTargetPub)`and clears`serverTargetPub`from memory.
- Client sends `(ciphertext, clientEncappedPub)`to server and the client is cleared from memory.
- Server assumes the authenticity of `clientEncappedPub`has been verified by the Ump policy engine.
- Server recovers plaintext by computing `DECRYPT(ciphertext, clientEncappedPub, clientTargetPriv)`and server target pair is cleared from memory. If the target pair is used multiple times we increase the count of messages that an attacker with the compromised target private key can decrypt.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-profile)Security profile

[§](https://docs.rs#receiver-pre-flight-authentication)Receiver pre-flight authentication

We achieve recipient authentication for both the server and client:

- **Client to Server**: client verifies that the server’s target key is signed by the enclaveAuth key. This check is critical for import/export flows. If the client accepts key material (e.g. a wallet seed) from a malicious party, they might not realize they have the wrong wallet (compromised seed because known or with bad entropy). If the client encrypts their seed to a malicious party, they lose funds directly. This is NOT required for email recovery and authentication flows: the client can afford to decrypt and use a bad API key. A bad API key will simply produce an invalid signature when used.
- **Server to Client**: server relies on upstream checks by Ump + activity signing scheme to enforce rules that guarantee authenticity of the client’s target key. Specifically, when the client “sends” clientTargetPub it actually submits a signed payload (activity), and that payload must be signed with an existing credential persisted in org data.

[§](https://docs.rs#forward-secrecy)Forward secrecy

The underlying HPKE spec does not provide forward secrecy on the recipient side since the target key can be long lived. To improve forward secrecy we specify that the target key should only be used once by the sender and receiver. We cannot enforce this strictly on the client-side because a client may choose to reuse their key. We could implement timestamp-based validation or rate limiting client-side but it wouldn’t be a complete solution. For now we accept that a client can use an encryption bundle multiple times if it so desires. However we enforce one-time use of the key pair on the enclave side by deleting it once a successful decryption happens.

In addition, we also support long lived enclave side keys. This allows clients to reuse a stable enclave encryption target, which can be helpful to reduce communication overhead for scenarios that are latency or throughput sensitive. The library types that support this pattern are `server::ReusableEnclaveEncryptServerRecv` and `client::encrypt_to_server_target`. For enclave -> client messages, the client must still use `EnclaveEncryptClient`, which ensures forward secrecy as the clients target key is deleted after use.

[§](https://docs.rs#sender-authentication)Sender authentication

We use `OpMode` Base because the sender’s KEM private key is not long lived and thus does not need HPKE authentication. In order for this to be exploited one side’s private key data would have to be leaked or an attacker would need to spoof a message from the sender. Turnkey mitigates this attack by layering a signature from an authentication key over payloads that contain ciphertext + encappedPub. Note that in the case of client to server the authentication signature is implicitly verified by the Ump policy engine. Read more about HPKE asymmetric authentication [here](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9180#name-authentication-using-an-asy).

# turnkey_api_key_stamper - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/turnkey_api_key_stamper/0.9.0/turnkey_api_key_stamper/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#turnkey_api_key_stamper)turnkey_api_key_stamper

This crate contains structs and utilities to work with P-256 keys, which [Turnkey](https://docs.turnkey.com/) uses as a primary way of authentication.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-a-new-p-256-api-key)Creating a new P-256 API key

```
use turnkey_api_key_stamper::TurnkeyP256ApiKey;
let api_key = TurnkeyP256ApiKey::generate();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#loading-api-keys-from-env)Loading API keys from env

If you keep API keys in env vars, load it with `from_bytes` or `from_strings`:

```
use std::env;
use turnkey_api_key_stamper::TurnkeyP256ApiKey;
// Assuming the env var is a hex-encoded string
let api_private_key = env::var("TURNKEY_API_PRIVATE_KEY").expect("cannot load TURNKEY_API_PRIVATE_KEY");
let api_key = TurnkeyP256ApiKey::from_strings(api_private_key, None).expect("loading API key failed");
```
If you want to store API keys in `.env` files, use [ dotenvy](https://docs.rs/dotenvy/latest/dotenvy/).

[§](https://docs.rs#load-api-keys-from-files)Load API keys from files

If you have generated API keys with Turnkey’s [command-line tool](https://github.com/tkhq/tkcli) you can load them with:

```
use turnkey_api_key_stamper::TurnkeyP256ApiKey;
let api_key = TurnkeyP256ApiKey::from_files(
    "/home/user/.config/turnkey/keys/key.priv",
    Some("/home/user/.config/turnkey/keys/key.pub"
).expect("loading should succeed"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#creating-an-api-stamp-to-sign-turnkey-requests)Creating an API stamp to sign Turnkey requests

The API is straightforward, once you have a handle on an API key, call `stamp`:

```
use turnkey_api_key_stamper::{TurnkeyP256ApiKey, Stamp};
let api_key = TurnkeyP256ApiKey::generate();
let stamp = api_key.stamp("POST request body goes here".as_bytes());
```
The stamp produced is a base64-encoded value, ready to be used as a stamp header. See [our documentation](https://docs.turnkey.com/developer-reference/api-overview/stamps#api-keys) for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error handling

Errors are centralized in `StamperError`.

# ikigai_personal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ikigai-personal/0.3.0/ikigai_personal/

## Expand description

`ikigai-personal` — personal contexts for ikigai.

Late-bound, OS-backed resources under `urn:personal:*` — your contacts,
calendar, and free/busy availability — resolved through the local operating
system rather than a remote service, so the data never leaves the machine.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-support)Platform support

macOS is the first backend. **Windows and Linux are placeholders today**: the
crate *builds* on them, but the personal resources resolve to a clear
“not supported yet” error until their backends land (Windows: Microsoft Graph
/ Active Directory; Linux: LDAP / CalDAV / D-Bus). The macOS backend currently
returns clearly-labelled **sample data** pending the real Contacts/EventKit
integration.

[§](https://docs.rs#capability-scoping)Capability scoping

Access is gated by `urn:cap:` capability scopes (see `ikigai-core`’s
`Capability`). `urn:personal:calendar` projects on the capability: a holder of
`urn:cap:personal:calendar:read:detail` sees full detail; one with only
`…:read:freebusy` sees busy blocks (no titles or attendees); one with neither
is denied. That’s the data-minimization story — *“an agent books around my
week without ever learning what I’m doing”* — and it’s why detail and free/busy
are one resource with two capability-scoped views rather than two resources.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Calendar](https://docs.rs/struct.CalendarConfig.html)- Config
- Configuration for the consolidated-view calendar machinery — the
hand-editable file a host loads (conventionally
`~/.config/ikigai/calendar.json`).
- [Calendar](https://docs.rs/struct.CalendarInfo.html)- Info
- One native calendar, as the OS reports it.
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.EventInfo.html)- Info
- One calendar event, normalized from the OS store.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [availability](https://docs.rs/fn.availability.html)
- `availability`: the free/busy projection for a period — busy blocks only, gated on- `urn:cap:personal:calendar:read:freebusy`.
- [calendar](https://docs.rs/fn.calendar.html)
- `calendar`: real events for a period, projected on the capability — full detail with- `…:read:detail`(and a Turtle face via- `as=text/turtle`), free/busy with- `…:read:freebusy`, denied with neither.
- [calendar_](https://docs.rs/fn.calendar_config.html)- config
- `calendar:config`: the effective consolidated-view configuration the host loaded (view name, source allowlist, inbox, account) — or a pointer to create the file if none was found.
- [calendars](https://docs.rs/fn.calendars.html)
- `calendars`: the native calendar collection.- `Source`lists every calendar with its account;- `Sink`creates one —- `name=`(default: the configured view) on- `account=`(default: configured account, else iCloud, else the system default). Real EventKit; the first use may raise the macOS calendar-access prompt.
- [contacts](https://docs.rs/fn.contacts.html)
- `contacts`: the local address book, gated on- `urn:cap:personal:contacts:read`.
- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_supported.html)- supported
- Whether a personal backend is implemented for the platform this was built for.
- [platform_](https://docs.rs/fn.platform_name.html)- name
- The human-readable name of the platform this was built for.
- [space](https://docs.rs/fn.space.html)
- The personal-contexts space: binds the resources at `urn:personal:*`. The optional`CalendarConfig``~/.config/ikigai/calendar.json`) parameterizes the consolidated-view machinery;`None`leaves the read resources fully functional.

# fastrace 0.7.18 - Docs.rs

# Fastrace

Fastrace is a tracing library [100x faster](https://docs.rs#benchmarks) than others:

Features:

- [Extremely fast](https://docs.rs#benchmarks)
- [Rich features for logging](https://github.com/fast/fastrace/blob/main/examples/logging.rs)
- Compatible with [Jaeger](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-jaeger),[Datadog](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-datadog), and[OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/)

## Resources

## Getting Started

## In Libraries

Libraries should include `fastrace` as a dependency without enabling any extra features.

```
[]
 = "0.7"
```
Add a `trace` attribute to the function you want to trace. In this example, a `SpanRecord` will be collected every time the function is called, if the caller sets up a tracing context.

```
```
Libraries can set up an individual tracing context, regardless of whether the caller has already set up a tracing context or not. This can be achieved by using `Span::root()` to start a new trace and `Span::set_local_parent()` to set up a local context for the current thread.

The `func_path!()` macro can detect the function's full name, which is used as the name of the root span.

```
use *;
```
## In Applications

Applications should include `fastrace` as a dependency with the `enable` feature set. To disable `fastrace` statically, remove the `enable` feature.

```
[]
 = {  = "0.7",  = ["enable"] }
```
Applications should initialize a `Reporter` implementation early in the program's runtime. Span records generated before the reporter is initialized will be ignored. Before terminating, `flush()` should be called to ensure all collected span records are reported.

When the root span is dropped, all of its children spans and itself will be reported at once. Since then, it's recommended to create root spans for short tasks, such as handling a request, as shown in the example below. Otherwise, an endless trace will never be reported.

```
use Config;
use ConsoleReporter;
use *;
```
## Supported Rust Versions (MSRV 1.91.0)

Fastrace is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.91.0. The current Fastrace version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

## Reporters

Fastrace supports multiple out-of-box reporters to export spans:

- `fastrace-jaeger`- [Jaeger](https://www.jaegertracing.io/)
- `fastrace-datadog`- [Datadog](https://www.datadoghq.com/)
- `fastrace-opentelemetry`- [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/)

## Integrations

Fastrace provides integrations with popular libraries to handle context propagation automatically:

- [fastrace-futures](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-futures): Trace Stream from- `futures`
- [fastrace-axum](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-axum): Trace- `axum`
- [fastrace-poem](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-poem): Trace- `poem`
- [fastrace-reqwest](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-reqwest): Trace- `reqwest`
- [fastrace-tonic](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-tonic): Trace- `tonic`
- [fastrace-tower](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-tower): Trace- `tower`
- [fastrace-tracing](https://crates.io/crates/fastrace-tracing): Compatibility layer for- `tracing`

Feel free to open a PR and add your projects here:

## Migrating from tokio-tracing

If you're using the [tokio-tracing](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing) ecosystem and want to switch to fastrace for better performance, you can use [fastrace-tracing](https://github.com/fast/fastrace-tracing) to make the transition easier.

The `fastrace-tracing` crate provides a compatibility layer that lets you capture spans from libraries instrumented with `tokio-tracing` in two lines of code:

```
let subscriber = default.with;
set_global_default.unwrap;
```
For more details, refer to the [fastrace-tracing documentation](https://docs.rs/fastrace-tracing).

## FAQ

### Why is Fastrace so fast?

The maintainer of fastrace posts articles describing the details:

- [The Design of A High-performance Tracing Library in Rust (Chinese)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8xTaxC1RcXE)
- [How We Trace a KV Database with Less than 5% Performance Impact](https://en.pingcap.com/blog/how-we-trace-a-kv-database-with-less-than-5-percent-performance-impact/)

### What is library-level tracing?

Library-level tracing refers to the capability of incorporating tracing capabilities directly within libraries, as opposed to restricting them to application-level or system-level tracing.

Tracing can introduce overhead to a program's execution. While this is generally acceptable at the application level, where the added overhead is often insignificant compared to the overall execution time, it can be more problematic at the library level. Here, functions may be invoked frequently or performance may be critical, and the overhead from tracing can become substantial. As a result, tracing libraries not designed with speed and efficiency in mind may not be suitable for library-level tracing.

In the realm of the Fastrace library, library-level tracing is engineered to be fast and lightweight, resulting in zero overhead when it's not activated. This makes fastrace an excellent choice for use in performance-sensitive applications, and it can be seamlessly integrated into libraries in a similar fashion to the log crate, something other tracing libraries may not offer.

### How does Fastrace differ from other tracing libraries?

While many tracing libraries aim for extensive features, Fastrace prioritizes performance and simplicity.

For example, fastrace doesn't introduce new logging macros, e.g., `info!()` or `error!()`, but seamlessly integrates with the [ log](https://crates.io/crates/log) crate. This allows you to use existing logging macros and dependencies, with logs automatically attached to the current tracing span.

### Will fastrace incorporate 'level' for spans?

The concept of 'level' may not be an optimal feature for tracing systems. While `tokio-tracing` incorporates this feature, the underlying motivation for having levels in a span primarily revolves around performance. More specifically, it relates to the performance implications of tracing elements that are not of interest. However, tracing differs from logging in two key aspects:

- Disregarding a low-level span might inadvertently discard a high-level child span.
- The process of filtering, or 'level' as it's often called, in a tracing system should be applied to a trace as a whole rather than individual spans within a trace.

In this context, Fastrace offers a more efficient solution by filtering out entire traces that are not of interest through its unique [tail-sampling](https://opentelemetry.io/blog/2022/tail-sampling/) design. Therefore, the concept of 'level', borrowed directly from logging systems, may not be suitable for Fastrace.

## Benchmarks

**By different architectures:**

| x86-64 (Intel Broadwell) | x86-64 (Intel Skylake) | x86-64 (AMD Zen) | ARM (AWS Graviton2) | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tokio-tracing | 124x slower | 33x slower | 36x slower | 29x slower |
| rustracing | 45x slower | 10x slower | 11x slower | 9x slower |
| fastrace (baseline) | 1x (3.4us) | 1x (3.2us) | 1x (3.8us) | 1x (4.2us) |

**By creating a different number of spans:**

| 1 span | 10 spans | 100 spans | 1000 spans | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tokio-tracing | 19x slower | 61x slower | 124x slower | 151x slower |
| rustracing | 13x slower | 26x slower | 45x slower | 55x slower |
| fastrace (baseline) | 1x (0.4us) | 1x (0.8us) | 1x (3.4us) | 1x (27.8us) |

Detailed results are available in [etc/benchmark-result](https://github.com/fast/fastrace/tree/main/etc/benchmark-result).

# fastrace - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fastrace/0.7.18/target-redirect/fastrace/

## Expand description

`fastrace` is a high-performance, ergonomic, library-level timeline tracing library for Rust.

Unlike most tracing libraries which are primarily designed for instrumenting executables,
`fastrace` also accommodates the need for library instrumentation. It stands out due to
its extreme lightweight and fast performance compared to other tracing libraries. Moreover,
it has zero overhead when not enabled in the executable, making it a worry-free choice for
libraries concerned about unnecessary performance loss.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In Libraries

Libraries should include `fastrace` as a dependency without enabling any extra features.

```
[dependencies]
fastrace = "0.7"
```
Add a [ trace](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html) attribute to the function you want to trace. In this example, a

[will be collected every time the function is called, if a tracing context is set up by the caller.](https://docs.rs/collector/struct.SpanRecord.html)

`SpanRecord````
#[fastrace::trace]
pub fn send_request(req: HttpRequest) -> Result<(), Error> {
    // ...
}
```
Libraries are able to set up an individual tracing context, regardless of whether
the caller has set up a tracing context or not. This can be achieved by using
[ Span::root()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.root) to start a new trace and

[to set up a local context for the current thread.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent)

`Span::set_local_parent()`The [ func_path!()](https://docs.rs/macro.func_path.html) macro can detect the function’s full name, which is used as
the name of the root span.

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
pub fn send_request(req: HttpRequest) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let root = Span::root(func_path!(), SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
    // ...
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-applications)In Applications

Applications should include `fastrace` as a dependency with the `enable` feature
set. To disable `fastrace` statically, simply remove the `enable` feature.

```
[dependencies]
fastrace = { version ="0.7", features = ["enable"] }
```
Applications should initialize a [ Reporter](https://docs.rs/collector/trait.Reporter.html) implementation early in the program’s runtime.
Span records generated before the reporter is initialized will be ignored. Before
terminating,

[should be called to ensure all collected span records are reported.](https://docs.rs/fn.flush.html)

`flush()````
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
fn main() {
    fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
    loop {
        let root = Span::root("worker-loop", SpanContext::random());
        let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
        handle_request();
    }
    fastrace::flush();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#key-concepts)Key Concepts

`fastrace` operates through three types: [ Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpan.html)

`LocalSpan`[, each representing a different type of tracing record. The macro](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[is available to manage these types automatically. For](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html)

`trace`[instrumentation, necessary utilities are provided by](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)

`Future`[.](https://docs.rs/future/trait.FutureExt.html)

`FutureExt`[§](https://docs.rs#span)Span

A [ Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html) represents an individual unit of work. It contains:

- A name
- A start timestamp and duration
- A set of key-value properties
- A reference to a parent `Span`

A new `Span` can be started through [ Span::root()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.root), requiring the trace id and the
parent span id from a remote source. If there’s no remote parent span, the parent span
id is typically set to its default value of zero.

Once we have the root `Span`, we can create a child `Span` using [ Span::enter_with_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter_with_parent),
thereby establishing the reference relationship between the spans.

`Span` is thread-safe and can be sent across threads.

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root_span = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    {
        let child_span = Span::enter_with_parent("a child span", &root_span);
        // ...
        // child_span ends here.
    }
    // root_span ends here.
}
fastrace::flush();
```
Sometimes, passing a `Span` through a function to create a child `Span` can be inconvenient.
We can employ a thread-local approach to avoid an explicit argument passing in the function.
In fastrace, [ Span::set_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent) and

[serve this purpose.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter_with_local_parent)

`Span::enter_with_local_parent()`[ Span::set_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent) method sets

**a local context of the**for the current thread.

`Span`[accesses the parent](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter_with_local_parent)

`Span::enter_with_local_parent()``Span` from the local context
and creates a child `Span` with it.```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
{
    let root_span = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root_span.set_local_parent();
    foo();
    // root_span ends here.
}
fn foo() {
    // The parent of this span is `root`.
    let _child_span = Span::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
    // ...
    // _child_span ends here.
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#local-span)Local Span

In a clear single-thread execution flow, where we can ensure that the `Span` does
not cross threads, meaning:

- The `Span`is not sent to or shared by other threads
- In asynchronous code, the lifetime of the `Span`doesn’t cross an`.await`point

we can use `LocalSpan` as a substitute for `Span` to effectively reduce overhead
and greatly enhance performance.

However, there is a precondition: The creation of `LocalSpan` must take place
within **a local context of a  Span**, which is established by invoking the

[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent)

`Span::set_local_parent()`If the code spans multiple function calls, this isn’t always straightforward to
confirm if the precondition is met. As such, it’s recommended to invoke
[ Span::set_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent) immediately after the creation of

`Span`.After **a local context of a  Span** is set using

[, use](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent)

`Span::set_local_parent()`[to start a](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpan.html#method.enter_with_local_parent)

`LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent()``LocalSpan`, which then
becomes the new local parent.If no local context is set, the [ LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpan.html#method.enter_with_local_parent) will do nothing.

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
    {
        // The parent of this span is `root`.
        let _span1 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
        foo();
    }
}
fn foo() {
    // The parent of this span is `span1`.
    let _span2 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span of child span");
}
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#event)Event

[ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) represents a single point in time where something occurred during the execution of a
program.

An `Event` can be seen as a log record attached to a span.

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
    root.add_event(Event::new("event in root"));
    {
        let _span1 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
        LocalSpan::add_event(Event::new("event in span1"));
    }
}
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#macro)Macro

The attribute-macro [ trace](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html) helps to reduce boilerplate.

Note: For successful tracing a function using the [ trace](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html) macro, the function call should
occur within

**a local context of a**.

`Span`For more detailed usage instructions, please refer to [ trace](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html).

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
use pollster::block_on;
#[trace]
fn do_something(i: u64) {
    std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(i));
}
#[trace]
async fn do_something_async(i: u64) {
    futures_timer::Delay::new(std::time::Duration::from_millis(i)).await;
}
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
    do_something(100);
    block_on(
        async {
            do_something_async(100).await;
        }
        .in_span(Span::enter_with_local_parent("async_job")),
    );
}
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#reporter)Reporter

[ Reporter](https://docs.rs/collector/trait.Reporter.html) is responsible for reporting the span records to a remote agent,
such as Jaeger.

Executables should initialize a reporter implementation early in the program’s runtime. Span records generated before the reporter is initialized will be ignored.

For an easy start, `fastrace` offers a [ ConsoleReporter](https://docs.rs/collector/struct.ConsoleReporter.html) that prints span
records to stderr. For more advanced use, crates like

`fastrace-jaeger`, `fastrace-datadog`,
and `fastrace-opentelemetry` are available.The reporter runs in a background collector thread. [ Config::report_interval()](https://docs.rs/collector/struct.Config.html#method.report_interval) controls the

*maximum*interval between report cycles, but the reporter may be invoked earlier. Do not rely on it for precise scheduling or batching.

```
use std::time::Duration;
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
fastrace::set_reporter(
    ConsoleReporter,
    Config::default().report_interval(Duration::from_secs(1)),
);
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

`fastrace` is designed to be fast and lightweight, considering four scenarios:

-
**No Tracing**: If the feature`enable`is not set in the application,`fastrace`will be completely optimized away from the final executable binary, achieving zero overhead.
-
**Sample Tracing**: If`enable`is set in the application, but only a small portion of the traces are enabled via`Span::root()``Span::noop()`
-
**Full Tracing with Tail Sampling**: If`enable`is set in the application, and all traces are enabled, however, only a select few interesting tracing records (e.g., P99) are reported, while normal traces are dismissed by using`Span::cancel()`
-
**Full Tracing**: If`enable`is set in the application, and all traces are reported,`fastrace`performs 10x to 100x faster than other tracing libraries in this case.

fn main() {
    fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
    loop {
        let root = Span::root("worker-loop", SpanContext::random());
        let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
        handle_request();
    }
    fastrace::flush();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#key-concepts)Key Concepts

`fastrace` operates through three types: [ Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpan.html)

`LocalSpan`[, each representing a different type of tracing record. The macro](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[is available to manage these types automatically. For](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html)

`trace`[instrumentation, necessary utilities are provided by](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)

`Future`[.](https://docs.rs/future/trait.FutureExt.html)

`FutureExt`[§](https://docs.rs#span)Span

A [ Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html) represents an individual unit of work. It contains:

- A name
- A start timestamp and duration
- A set of key-value properties
- A reference to a parent `Span`

A new `Span` can be started through [ Span::root()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.root), requiring the trace id and the
parent span id from a remote source. If there’s no remote parent span, the parent span
id is typically set to its default value of zero.

Once we have the root `Span`, we can create a child `Span` using [ Span::enter_with_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter_with_parent),
thereby establishing the reference relationship between the spans.

`Span` is thread-safe and can be sent across threads.

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root_span = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    {
        let child_span = Span::enter_with_parent("a child span", &root_span);
        // ...
        // child_span ends here.
    }
    // root_span ends here.
}
fastrace::flush();
```
Sometimes, passing a `Span` through a function to create a child `Span` can be inconvenient.
We can employ a thread-local approach to avoid an explicit argument passing in the function.
In fastrace, [ Span::set_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent) and

[serve this purpose.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter_with_local_parent)

`Span::enter_with_local_parent()`[ Span::set_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent) method sets

**a local context of the**for the current thread.

`Span`[accesses the parent](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter_with_local_parent)

`Span::enter_with_local_parent()``Span` from the local context
and creates a child `Span` with it.```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
{
    let root_span = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root_span.set_local_parent();
    foo();
    // root_span ends here.
}
fn foo() {
    // The parent of this span is `root`.
    let _child_span = Span::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
    // ...
    // _child_span ends here.
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#local-span)Local Span

In a clear single-thread execution flow, where we can ensure that the `Span` does
not cross threads, meaning:

- The `Span`is not sent to or shared by other threads
- In asynchronous code, the lifetime of the `Span`doesn’t cross an`.await`point

we can use `LocalSpan` as a substitute for `Span` to effectively reduce overhead
and greatly enhance performance.

However, there is a precondition: The creation of `LocalSpan` must take place
within **a local context of a  Span**, which is established by invoking the

[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent)

`Span::set_local_parent()`If the code spans multiple function calls, this isn’t always straightforward to
confirm if the precondition is met. As such, it’s recommended to invoke
[ Span::set_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent) immediately after the creation of

`Span`.After **a local context of a  Span** is set using

[, use](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.set_local_parent)

`Span::set_local_parent()`[to start a](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpan.html#method.enter_with_local_parent)

`LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent()``LocalSpan`, which then
becomes the new local parent.If no local context is set, the [ LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent()](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpan.html#method.enter_with_local_parent) will do nothing.

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
    {
        // The parent of this span is `root`.
        let _span1 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
        foo();
    }
}
fn foo() {
    // The parent of this span is `span1`.
    let _span2 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span of child span");
}
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#event)Event

[ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) represents a single point in time where something occurred during the execution of a
program.

An `Event` can be seen as a log record attached to a span.

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
    root.add_event(Event::new("event in root"));
    {
        let _span1 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
        LocalSpan::add_event(Event::new("event in span1"));
    }
}
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#macro)Macro

The attribute-macro [ trace](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html) helps to reduce boilerplate.

Note: For successful tracing a function using the [ trace](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html) macro, the function call should
occur within

**a local context of a**.

`Span`For more detailed usage instructions, please refer to [ trace](https://docs.rs/attr.trace.html).

```
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
use pollster::block_on;
#[trace]
fn do_something(i: u64) {
    std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(i));
}
#[trace]
async fn do_something_async(i: u64) {
    futures_timer::Delay::new(std::time::Duration::from_millis(i)).await;
}
fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
{
    let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
    let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
    do_something(100);
    block_on(
        async {
            do_something_async(100).await;
        }
        .in_span(Span::enter_with_local_parent("async_job")),
    );
}
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#reporter)Reporter

[ Reporter](https://docs.rs/collector/trait.Reporter.html) is responsible for reporting the span records to a remote agent,
such as Jaeger.

Executables should initialize a reporter implementation early in the program’s runtime. Span records generated before the reporter is initialized will be ignored.

For an easy start, `fastrace` offers a [ ConsoleReporter](https://docs.rs/collector/struct.ConsoleReporter.html) that prints span
records to stderr. For more advanced use, crates like

`fastrace-jaeger`, `fastrace-datadog`,
and `fastrace-opentelemetry` are available.The reporter runs in a background collector thread. [ Config::report_interval()](https://docs.rs/collector/struct.Config.html#method.report_interval) controls the

*maximum*interval between report cycles, but the reporter may be invoked earlier. Do not rely on it for precise scheduling or batching.

```
use std::time::Duration;
use fastrace::collector::Config;
use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
fastrace::set_reporter(
    ConsoleReporter,
    Config::default().report_interval(Duration::from_secs(1)),
);
fastrace::flush();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

`fastrace` is designed to be fast and lightweight, considering four scenarios:

-
**No Tracing**: If the feature`enable`is not set in the application,`fastrace`will be completely optimized away from the final executable binary, achieving zero overhead.
-
**Sample Tracing**: If`enable`is set in the application, but only a small portion of the traces are enabled via`Span::root()``Span::noop()`
-
**Full Tracing with Tail Sampling**: If`enable`is set in the application, and all traces are enabled, however, only a select few interesting tracing records (e.g., P99) are reported, while normal traces are dismissed by using`Span::cancel()`
-
**Full Tracing**: If`enable`is set in the application, and all traces are reported,`fastrace`performs 10x to 100x faster than other tracing libraries in this case.

- [file_](https://docs.rs/macro.file_location.html)- location
- Get the source file location where the macro is invoked. Returns a `&'static str`.
- [full_](https://docs.rs/macro.full_name.html)- name - Deprecated
- Get the full path of the function where the macro is invoked. Returns a `&'static str`.
- [func_](https://docs.rs/macro.func_name.html)- name
- Get the name of the function where the macro is invoked. Returns a `&'static str`.
- [func_](https://docs.rs/macro.func_path.html)- path
- Get the full path of the function where the macro is invoked. Returns a `&'static str`.

- A thread-safe span.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [flush](https://docs.rs/fn.flush.html)
- Flushes all pending span records to the reporter immediately.

- Sets the reporter and its configuration for the current application.

# fastrace/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// Copyright 2020 TiKV Project Authors. Licensed under Apache-2.0.
[2](https://docs.rs#2)
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! `fastrace` is a high-performance, ergonomic, library-level timeline tracing library for Rust.
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! Unlike most tracing libraries which are primarily designed for instrumenting executables,
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! `fastrace` also accommodates the need for library instrumentation. It stands out due to
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! its extreme lightweight and fast performance compared to other tracing libraries. Moreover,
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! it has zero overhead when not enabled in the executable, making it a worry-free choice for
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! libraries concerned about unnecessary performance loss.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! # Getting Started
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! ## In Libraries
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! Libraries should include `fastrace` as a dependency without enabling any extra features.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! ```toml
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! [dependencies]
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! fastrace = "0.7"
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! ```
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! Add a [`trace`] attribute to the function you want to trace. In this example, a
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! [`SpanRecord`] will be collected every time the function is called, if a tracing context
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! is set up by the caller.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! ```
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! # struct HttpRequest;
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! # struct Error;
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! #[fastrace::trace]
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! pub fn send_request(req: HttpRequest) -> Result<(), Error> {
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!     // ...
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!     # Ok(())
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! }
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! ```
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! Libraries are able to set up an individual tracing context, regardless of whether
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! the caller has set up a tracing context or not. This can be achieved by using
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! [`Span::root()`] to start a new trace and [`Span::set_local_parent()`] to set up a
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! local context for the current thread.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! The [`func_path!()`] macro can detect the function's full name, which is used as
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! the name of the root span.
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! ```
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! use fastrace::prelude::*;
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! # struct HttpRequest;
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! # struct Error;
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! pub fn send_request(req: HttpRequest) -> Result<(), Error> {
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!     let root = Span::root(func_path!(), SpanContext::random());
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     // ...
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!     # Ok(())
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! }
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! ```
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! ## In Applications
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//!
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! Applications should include `fastrace` as a dependency with the `enable` feature
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! set. To disable `fastrace` statically, simply remove the `enable` feature.
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! ```toml
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! [dependencies]
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! fastrace = { version ="0.7", features = ["enable"] }
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! ```
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! Applications should initialize a [`Reporter`] implementation early in the program's runtime.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! Span records generated before the reporter is initialized will be ignored. Before
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! terminating, [`flush()`] should be called to ensure all collected span records are reported.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! ```
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! use fastrace::collector::Config;
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! use fastrace::prelude::*;
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! fn main() {
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     loop {
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!         let root = Span::root("worker-loop", SpanContext::random());
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!         let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!         handle_request();
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!         # break;
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     }
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!     fastrace::flush();
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! }
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! # fn handle_request() {}
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! ```
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! # Key Concepts
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! `fastrace` operates through three types: [`Span`], [`LocalSpan`], and [`Event`], each
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! representing a different type of tracing record. The macro [`trace`] is available to
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! manage these types automatically. For [`Future`] instrumentation, necessary utilities
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! are provided by [`FutureExt`].
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! ## Span
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! A [`Span`] represents an individual unit of work. It contains:
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! - A name
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! - A start timestamp and duration
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! - A set of key-value properties
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! - A reference to a parent `Span`
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! A new `Span` can be started through [`Span::root()`], requiring the trace id and the
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! parent span id from a remote source. If there's no remote parent span, the parent span
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! id is typically set to its default value of zero.
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! Once we have the root `Span`, we can create a child `Span` using [`Span::enter_with_parent()`],
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! thereby establishing the reference relationship between the spans.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! `Span` is thread-safe and can be sent across threads.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! ```
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! use fastrace::collector::Config;
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! use fastrace::prelude::*;
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! {
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!     let root_span = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!     {
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!         let child_span = Span::enter_with_parent("a child span", &root_span);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!         // ...
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!         // child_span ends here.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!     }
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     // root_span ends here.
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! fastrace::flush();
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! ```
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! Sometimes, passing a `Span` through a function to create a child `Span` can be inconvenient.
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! We can employ a thread-local approach to avoid an explicit argument passing in the function.
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! In fastrace, [`Span::set_local_parent()`] and [`Span::enter_with_local_parent()`] serve this
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! purpose.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! [`Span::set_local_parent()`] method sets __a local context of the `Span`__ for the current
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! thread. [`Span::enter_with_local_parent()`] accesses the parent `Span` from the local context
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! and creates a child `Span` with it.
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! ```
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! use fastrace::prelude::*;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!

[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     let _guard = root_span.set_local_parent();
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!     foo();
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     // root_span ends here.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! fn foo() {
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     // The parent of this span is `root`.
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!     let _child_span = Span::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!     // ...
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!     // _child_span ends here.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! }
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! ```
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! ## Local Span
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! In a clear single-thread execution flow, where we can ensure that the `Span` does
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! not cross threads, meaning:
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! - The `Span` is not sent to or shared by other threads
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! - In asynchronous code, the lifetime of the `Span` doesn't cross an `.await` point
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! we can use `LocalSpan` as a substitute for `Span` to effectively reduce overhead
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! and greatly enhance performance.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! However, there is a precondition: The creation of `LocalSpan` must take place
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! within __a local context of a `Span`__, which is established by invoking the
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! [`Span::set_local_parent()`] method.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! If the code spans multiple function calls, this isn't always straightforward to
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! confirm if the precondition is met. As such, it's recommended to invoke
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! [`Span::set_local_parent()`] immediately after the creation of `Span`.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! After __a local context of a `Span`__ is set using [`Span::set_local_parent()`],
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! use [`LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent()`] to start a `LocalSpan`, which then
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! becomes the new local parent.
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! If no local context is set, the [`LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent()`] will do nothing.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! ```
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! use fastrace::collector::Config;
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! use fastrace::prelude::*;
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!     let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!     let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!     {
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!         // The parent of this span is `root`.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!         let _span1 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//!         foo();
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!     }
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! }
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! fn foo() {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!     // The parent of this span is `span1`.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!     let _span2 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span of child span");
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! }
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! fastrace::flush();
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! ```
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! ## Event
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//!
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! [`Event`] represents a single point in time where something occurred during the execution of a
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! program.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! An `Event` can be seen as a log record attached to a span.
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! ```
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! use fastrace::collector::Config;
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! use fastrace::prelude::*;
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!     let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!     let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//!     root.add_event(Event::new("event in root"));
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!     {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!         let _span1 = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!         LocalSpan::add_event(Event::new("event in span1"));
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!     }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! fastrace::flush();
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! ```
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! ## Macro
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! The attribute-macro [`trace`] helps to reduce boilerplate.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! Note: For successful tracing a function using the [`trace`] macro, the function call should
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! occur within __a local context of a `Span`__.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! For more detailed usage instructions, please refer to [`trace`].
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! ```
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! use fastrace::collector::Config;
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! use fastrace::prelude::*;
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! use pollster::block_on;
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! #[trace]
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! fn do_something(i: u64) {
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!     std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(i));
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! }
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! #[trace]
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! async fn do_something_async(i: u64) {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!     futures_timer::Delay::new(std::time::Duration::from_millis(i)).await;
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! }
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//!
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! fastrace::set_reporter(ConsoleReporter, Config::default());
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//!     let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!     let _guard = root.set_local_parent();
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!     do_something(100);
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//!
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//!     block_on(
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!         async {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!             do_something_async(100).await;
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!         }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!         .in_span(Span::enter_with_local_parent("async_job")),
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//!     );
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//!
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! fastrace::flush();
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! ```
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! ## Reporter
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! [`Reporter`] is responsible for reporting the span records to a remote agent,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! such as Jaeger.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! Executables should initialize a reporter implementation early in the program's
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! runtime. Span records generated before the reporter is initialized will be ignored.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! For an easy start, `fastrace` offers a [`ConsoleReporter`] that prints span
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! records to stderr. For more advanced use, crates like `fastrace-jaeger`, `fastrace-datadog`,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//! and `fastrace-opentelemetry` are available.
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! The reporter runs in a background collector thread. [`Config::report_interval()`] controls the
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//! *maximum* interval between report cycles, but the reporter may be invoked earlier. Do not rely
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! on it for precise scheduling or batching.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! ```
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! use std::time::Duration;
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//! use fastrace::collector::Config;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! use fastrace::collector::ConsoleReporter;
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! fastrace::set_reporter(
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!     ConsoleReporter,
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//!     Config::default().report_interval(Duration::from_secs(1)),
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! );
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! fastrace::flush();
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! ```
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! # Performance
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//!
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//! `fastrace` is designed to be fast and lightweight, considering four scenarios:
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! - **No Tracing**: If the feature `enable` is not set in the application, `fastrace` will be
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!   completely optimized away from the final executable binary, achieving zero overhead.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//!
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! - **Sample Tracing**: If `enable` is set in the application, but only a small portion of the
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//!   traces are enabled via [`Span::root()`], while the other portions are started with
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//!   placeholders using [`Span::noop()`]. The overhead in this case is very small - merely an
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!   integer load, comparison, and jump.
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//!
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! - **Full Tracing with Tail Sampling**: If `enable` is set in the application, and all traces are
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//!   enabled, however, only a select few interesting tracing records (e.g., P99) are reported,
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!   while normal traces are dismissed by using [`Span::cancel()`] to avoid being reported, the
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//!   overhead of collecting traces is still very small. This could be useful when you are
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//!   interested in examining program's tail latency.
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//!
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! - **Full Tracing**: If `enable` is set in the application, and all traces are reported,
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//!   `fastrace` performs 10x to 100x faster than other tracing libraries in this case.
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//!
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//!
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//! [`Span`]: crate::Span

# trace in fastrace - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fastrace/0.7.18/fastrace/attr.trace.html

`#[trace]`## Expand description

An attribute macro designed to eliminate boilerplate code.

This macro automatically creates a span for the annotated function. The span name defaults to
the function name but can be customized by passing a string literal as an argument using the
`name` parameter.

The `#[trace]` attribute requires a local parent context to function correctly. Ensure that
the function annotated with `#[trace]` is called within **a local context of a  Span**, which
is established by invoking the

`Span::set_local_parent()` method.[§](https://docs.rs#arguments)Arguments

- `name`- The name of the span. Defaults to the full path of the function.
- `short_name`- Whether to use the function name without path as the span name. Defaults to- `false`.
- `enter_on_poll`- Whether to enter the span on poll. If set to- `false`,- `in_span`will be used. Only available for- `async fn`. Defaults to- `false`.
- `properties`- A list of key-value pairs to be added as properties to the span. The value can be a format string, where the function arguments are accessible. Defaults to- `{}`.
- `crate`- The path to the fastrace crate. Defaults to- `::fastrace`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
#[trace]
fn simple() {
    // ...
}
#[trace(short_name = true)]
async fn simple_async() {
    // ...
}
#[trace(name = "qux", enter_on_poll = true)]
async fn baz() {
    // ...
}
#[trace(properties = { "k1": "v1", "a": "argument `a` is {a:?}" })]
async fn properties(a: u64) {
    // ...
}
```
The code snippets above will be expanded to:

```
fn simple() {
    let __guard__ = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("example::simple");
    // ...
}
async fn simple_async() {
    let __span__ = Span::enter_with_local_parent("simple_async");
    async {
        // ...
    }
    .in_span(__span__)
    .await
}
async fn baz() {
    async {
        // ...
    }
    .enter_on_poll("qux")
    .await
}
async fn properties(a: u64) {
    let __span__ = Span::enter_with_local_parent("example::properties").with_properties(|| {
        [
            (std::borrow::Cow::from("k1"), std::borrow::Cow::from("v1")),
            (
                std::borrow::Cow::from("a"),
                std::borrow::Cow::from(format!("argument `a` is {a:?}")),
            ),
        ]
    });
    async {
        // ...
    }
    .in_span(__span__)
    .await
}
```

# Span in fastrace - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fastrace/0.7.18/fastrace/struct.Span.html

`pub struct Span {}`## Expand description

A thread-safe span.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new trace and return its root span.

Once dropped, the root span automatically submits all associated child spans to the reporter.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
```
Create a new child span associated with the specified parent span.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
let child = Span::enter_with_parent("child", &root);
```

Multiple-parent spans are deprecated. Use `enter_with_parent` and link other parents with `with_link`.

Create a new child span associated with multiple parent spans.

This API is deprecated. The first non-noop parent becomes the primary parent; any additional parents are attached as links.

Use [ Span::enter_with_parent](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter_with_parent) plus

[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.with_link)

`Span::with_link`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
let parent1 = Span::root("parent1", SpanContext::random());
let parent2 = Span::root("parent2", SpanContext::random());
let child = Span::enter_with_parent("child", &parent1)
    .with_link(SpanContext::from_span(&parent2).unwrap());
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fastrace/span.rs.html#463-470)#### pub fn [push_child_spans](https://docs.rs#method.push_child_spans)(&self, local_spans: [LocalSpans](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpans.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fastrace/span.rs.html#463-470)

#### pub fn [push_child_spans](https://docs.rs#method.push_child_spans)(&self, local_spans: [LocalSpans](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpans.html))

Attach a collection of [ LocalSpan](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalSpan.html) instances as child spans to the current span.

This method allows you to associate previously collected `LocalSpan` instances with the
current span. This is particularly useful when the `LocalSpan` instances were initiated
before their parent span, and were collected manually using a [ LocalCollector](https://docs.rs/local/struct.LocalCollector.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```
use fastrace::local::LocalCollector;
use fastrace::prelude::*;
// Collect local spans manually without a parent
let collector = LocalCollector::start();
let span = LocalSpan::enter_with_local_parent("a child span");
drop(span);
let local_spans = collector.collect();
// Attach the local spans to a parent
let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
root.push_child_spans(local_spans);
```
Returns the elapsed time since the span was created. If the `Span` is a noop span,
this function will return `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
use std::time::Duration;
let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
// ...
if root
    .elapsed()
    .map(|elapsed| elapsed < Duration::from_secs(1))
    .unwrap_or(false)
{
    root.cancel();
}
```
Dismisses the trace, preventing the reporting of any span records associated with it.

This is particularly useful when focusing on the tail latency of a program. For instant, you can dismiss all traces finishes within the 99th percentile.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Trace cancellation is best-effort. Spans are held until the root span finishes, so calling
`cancel()` on the root span will discard spans already collected (and those collected until
the root span is dropped). Spans submitted after the root span finishes may still be
reported because there is no longer an active collector to associate them with the
cancelled trace.

This method only dismisses the entire trace when called on the root span. If called on a non-root span, it will do nothing.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
root.cancel();
```

# fastrace::future - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fastrace/0.7.18/fastrace/future/index.html

## Expand description

This module provides tools to trace a `Future`.

The [ FutureExt](https://docs.rs/trait.FutureExt.html) trait extends

`Future` with two methods: [and](https://docs.rs/(FutureExt::in_span))

`in_span()`[. It is crucial that the outermost future uses](https://docs.rs/(FutureExt::enter_on_poll))

`enter_on_poll()``in_span()`,
otherwise, the traces inside the `Future` will be lost.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use fastrace::prelude::*;
let root = Span::root("root", SpanContext::random());
// Instrument the a task
let task = async {
    async {
        // ...
    }
    .enter_on_poll("future is polled")
    .await;
}
.in_span(Span::enter_with_parent("task", &root));
runtime.spawn(task);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Enter](https://docs.rs/struct.EnterOnPoll.html)- OnPoll
- Adapter for `FutureExt::enter_on_poll()`
- [InSpan](https://docs.rs/struct.InSpan.html)
- Adapter for `FutureExt::in_span()`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Future](https://docs.rs/trait.FutureExt.html)- Ext
- An extension trait for `Futures`that provides tracing instrument adapters.

use fastrace::file_location;
fn foo() {

    let column = parts.next().unwrap();
    let line = parts.next().unwrap();
